newsitem.title: GERMANY: Workers protest as Bonn nears post monopoly deal.
newsitem.headline: Workers protest as Bonn nears post monopoly deal.

text.p: Around 23,000 German postal workers converged on Bonn in a convoy of buses on Monday to protest against plans by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government for far-reaching postal liberalisation.

The demonstrators gathered at the headquarters of Kohl's junior coalition partner Free Democrats (FDP), who have called for ending the postal monopoly as soon as possible, and follow work stoppages at post offices in 52 cities last week.

The postal workers union, Deutsche Postgewerkschaft (DPG), organising the march said tens of thousands of jobs would be lost if the postal monopoly was completely removed in 1998 and contribute to Germany's spiralling unemployment crisis.

But as the protestors waved placards and delivered 300,000 postcards from supporters of "a modern, reliable post office for all" to the Post Ministry, the ruling coalition seemed to have already made up its mind to curtail the current monopoly.

Government coalition sources said Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the FDP had agreed to grant Deutsche Post AG a monopoly extension for up to five years on letters weighing up to 100 grams (3.5 ounces).

That is well below the 350 grams (12.4 ounces) originally supported by Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch and reflects the influence of the free market forces in the FDP, who demonstrators called the "grave diggers of the post office."
Post Ministry State Secretary Gerhard Pfeffermann said Boetsch had signalled that a 100 gram limit would be an acceptable compromise.

FDP parliamentary post spokesman Paul Friedhoff said allowing Deutsche Post to maintain its monopoly on letters weighing less than 350 grams until the end of 2002 would mean only two percent of post would actually be open to competition.
The sources, who declined to be named, said a decision had yet to be reached on whether the licence should last for four or five years before full competition.

The Bonn government is due to discuss on Tuesday a draft law that would sweep aside the centuries-old monopoly set up by the Thurn and Taxis aristocracy which laid the basis for modern postal delivery in the 17th century.
But Deutsche Post chairman Klaus Zumwinkel appealed to Finance Minister Theo Waigel to keep the monopoly on letters under 350 grams or risk failure of the planned privatisation.
Zumwinkel said if the post office lost its monopoly next year the company would sink into debt and be unsaleable.
The DPG said the Bonn plans would lead to a "poorer, scaled-down, and more expensive postal service".

The union fears the new postal law will open the market up to "cherry-picking", in which rivals will be able to operate in the most lucrative markets, ignoring less attractive market segments, such as delivery to remote locations.
But Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, an FDP member, said the removal of the monopoly should create new jobs in small and medium sized firms competing against Deutsche Post.
"Those protesting against the new post law are hindering the creation of new, modern jobs in the service sector," he said in a statement.
The German Association of Post Customers said the postal monopoly had to fall for the benefit of consumers.
"It comes down to weighing up the interests of around 300,000 postal workers against those of 80 million citizens," association head Wilhelm Huebner said.
